items.title: We Baked Some Tudor Pastries | Historical Cookery at Kew
items.description: Today's recipe dates from the 1780s: Richard Briggs’ ‘Maids of Honour Tarts’. But the origin story is somewhat controversial. This recipe has been attributed to many different people over the years – including Anne Boleyn’s maid of honour. The story goes that Henry VIII came across some maids eating the tarts. He thought they were so good that he had the baker imprisoned and the recipe locked away in an iron box only to be produced for the royal family. In fact, there are recipes for curd tarts

featured_read.title: Blackie & Co.: A Blackbird’s Lesson in Friendship
featured_read.snippet: In the middle of my bleakest winter, my friend Andrea gave me a battered copy of a forgotten book from her elderly father’s used bookshop in rural Texas, by a man named Hockley Clarke. I inhaled it in a day. Born in England in the final year of the nineteenth century, Hockley Clarke grew up loving nature.
featured_read.blurb: A forgotten naturalist's memoir becomes the unlikely medicine for a bleak winter — this is a quiet meditation on what a wild creature can teach us about the art of paying attention to one another. Set aside your afternoon for it.

garden_note.note: High summer in Zürich settles into its richest, heaviest hour tonight — the cutting garden is almost embarrassingly full, and the tomatoes on the south wall have finally decided they mean business. Step outside after supper and let the evening warmth linger; August is one day away and the light, though you can't quite feel it yet, has already begun its slow, graceful retreat.
